h1: The 8 Best Budget Server Racks for Home Labs and Small Offices, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Budget Server Racks: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 8 budget open-frame server and network racks from 12U to 30U, scored on depth range, load rating, casters and build.
summary: The VEVOR 12U with adjustable 23 to 40 inch depth is the best budget rack for most home labs, because it fits both shallow switches and deep servers and comes with casters and a grounding wire. The GlobalRack 27U is the pick for a bigger build with a 1200 lb rating, and the RIVECO 25U is the sturdiest rivet-built frame. The AxcessAbles racks suit network gear, not deep servers.
intro: Rack height gets all the attention, but depth is what wrecks most budget purchases. A 12U rack sounds roomy until a 28 inch deep server will not fit inside an 18 inch deep frame, and by then the rack is already bolted together. Network switches and patch panels are shallow and will sit in almost anything, while real rack servers and some NAS chassis need 24 to 30 inches of rail depth. Decide what the deepest device is, then pick the rack.

This ranking sorts eight open-frame racks by that logic. We reviewed listings for height in U, usable depth, load rating on feet and on casters, steel gauge, shelves and hardware included. Load ratings differ between a fixed rack on its feet, a wall-mounted one and one on wheels, so we note which figure applies. Everything is from listings, and we skip dimensions that are not stated.

products.name: VEVOR 12U Open Frame Server Rack, 23-40in Adjustable Depth
products.verdict: Twelve rack units, 23 to 40 inches of adjustable depth, casters and a grounding wire.
products.description:
The VEVOR 12U rack has an adjustable depth of 23 to 40 inches, a 500 lb capacity on the ground and 150 lb on a wall, and ships with casters and a grounding wire. Its price is in the $50 to $100 range.

It wins because the depth range makes it fit nearly everything. At 23 inches minimum it handles most servers, and at 40 inches it takes deep storage chassis that would not fit the 18 inch racks in this ranking. Twelve units is the right size for a home lab with a switch, a patch panel, a firewall, a NAS and a small UPS. The grounding wire is a small but proper detail for electrical safety, and casters let you roll it out for cabling. The cost of that flexibility is a footprint that is deeper than the fixed racks.

Buy it for a first home lab where you do not yet know what you will rack. Keep heavy gear low and the rack on level floor.
products.idealFor: Home lab builders who need to fit both shallow and deep gear.
products.skipIf: You need more than 12U of space.

products.name: GlobalRack 27U Open Frame Server Rack, with Wheels
products.verdict: 27U with a 1200 lb rating, 22 to 35 inch depth and square holes with M6 hardware.
products.description:
The GlobalRack stands 43.5 inches high with 27U of space, adjusts from 22 to 35 inches deep and carries 1200 lbs. It has pre-installed square holes, includes M6 hardware and rolls on wheels. It costs between $100 and $200.

It takes second place because it gives you the most room and the highest rating in the group. Square mounting holes accept cage nuts, which is how most modern servers and switches fasten, and M6 hardware is the standard for them. A 22 to 35 inch range covers most rack servers. At 43.5 inches tall it is shorter than a full-height rack, so it fits under low ceilings or in a closet. It ranks below the VEVOR only because the minimum depth is 22 inches, which leaves out the shallowest gear for tidy mounting, and it is a larger purchase.

Choose it for a growing lab with several servers. Check that the 1200 lb figure applies to a static load, not a rolling one.
products.idealFor: Growing labs with several servers and storage units.
products.skipIf: You only have a few small devices.

products.name: AxcessAbles 12U Network Rack with Wheels, 500lb Capacity, 18" Depth
products.verdict: A rolling 12U rack with 18 inches of usable depth and a 1.5mm steel frame.
products.description:
The AxcessAbles 12U has 18 inches of usable depth, a 1.5mm steel frame, a 550 lb rated capacity and 3 inch locking casters. It is priced at $100 to $200, though the title quotes 500 lbs.

It ranks third because it is built for the gear most home setups actually use: switches, patch panels, routers and shallow appliances. An 18 inch depth rules out deep servers, so know your hardware. The 1.5mm steel is a respectable gauge for the price, and locking casters keep the rack from creeping when you plug cables in. The two capacity figures differ slightly between title and spec, so assume the lower number.

Buy it for a network closet or small office. If you plan to rack a full-depth server, choose a rack with adjustable depth.
cons: Capacity figures differ in the listing
products.idealFor: Network closets and small offices with switches and patch panels.
products.skipIf: You need to mount full-depth servers.

products.name: RIVECO 25U Server Rack Adjustable Depth, 1400 LBS
products.verdict: All-rivet 25U frame with 20 to 30 inch depth and 880 lb capacity on its feet.
products.description:
The RIVECO 25U adjusts from 20 to 30 inches deep, is rated for 880 lbs on its feet and 660 lbs on casters, and uses all-rivet construction. Cable rings are included, and the title advertises 1400 lbs. It costs $200 to $500.

It ranks fourth because riveted joints, which are permanent, do not loosen with vibration the way a bolted frame can, and that suits a rack that will carry a lot of weight. The honest rating is the one in the specs, 880 lbs on feet, rather than the 1400 lb headline. It is pricier than the others of its height and gives up the 40 inch depth of the VEVOR.

Pick it if you want a sturdy, permanent frame for a mid-size server install. Plan to keep it in one place, because a riveted rack cannot be broken down for moving.
cons: Headline 1400 lb is not the real rating
products.idealFor: Mid-size installs that stay put and carry real weight.
products.skipIf: You may need to move or reconfigure the rack.

products.name: Tecmojo 12U Open Frame Network Rack, Floor or Wall Mount
products.verdict: A cold rolled steel 12U frame for floor or wall, with two vented shelves in the box.
products.description:
The Tecmojo is a 12U open-frame rack made from cold rolled steel, rated for 260 lbs on the floor and 130 lbs on a wall. It comes with two vented 1U shelves and lists a $50 to $100 price.

It ranks fifth because its ratings are the lowest of the 12U racks, but it delivers the shelves, which most others charge extra for. Two vented shelves are useful for devices that do not rack mount, such as a modem or a mini PC. The wall option makes it good for a tight closet, though 130 lbs on a wall demands solid studs or masonry anchors. It gives up the casters and the depth adjustability of the VEVOR.

Buy it for a lightweight network setup on a wall or floor. Do not use it for heavy servers or a rack full of drives.
cons: Lowest load ratings of the 12U racks
products.idealFor: Lightweight network setups in a closet or on a wall.
products.skipIf: You will rack heavy servers or drives.

products.name: VEVOR 20U Open Frame Server Rack, 23-40in Adjustable Depth
products.verdict: Twenty units and the same 23 to 40 inch depth, but only a 200 lb ground rating.
products.description:
The VEVOR 20U shares the 23 to 40 inch adjustable depth of the 12U model, carries 200 lbs on the ground and 150 lbs on a wall, and includes a grounding wire and a full hardware kit. It costs $100 to $200.

It ranks sixth because the load rating is the problem. At 200 lbs on the ground, the 20U carries less than the 12U sibling's 500 lbs, so tall racks must be filled with light gear. A fully loaded rack can tip if it is top-heavy, so keep heavy items at the bottom. The extra height is useful if you have lots of switches and patch panels.

Choose it if you need 20U for light network gear. For heavier servers, pick the GlobalRack or RIVECO instead.
products.idealFor: Light network gear that needs more than 12U.
products.skipIf: You plan to rack heavy servers.

products.name: AxcessAbles 22U Rolling IT Server Rack, 550LB Heavy Duty Open Frame
products.verdict: A 22U rolling frame, 18 inches deep, with removable vented side panels.
products.description:
The AxcessAbles 22U is 18 inches deep, made of textured matte black steel, and rated for 550 lbs static and 440 lbs when rolling. It comes with removable vented side panels and falls in the $200 to $500 range.

It ranks seventh because the money buys height and finish rather than flexibility. Removable vented panels give the frame a more finished appearance in an office and keep dust and fingers out while still letting air through. Eighteen inches of depth limits the hardware to network gear and shallow devices. It costs more than the 12U version without adding depth.

Buy it for a visible office rack of network equipment that needs side panels. Skip it for deep servers.
products.idealFor: Office racks of network gear that benefit from side panels.
products.skipIf: You need to fit deep servers.

products.name: AxcessAbles 30U Rolling Network Server Rack, 550LB Capacity
products.verdict: A 30U rolling rack with the same 550 lb static rating and 18 inch depth.
products.description:
The 30U AxcessAbles is 18 inches deep with a capacity of 550 lbs static and 440 lbs when rolling, plus removable vented side panels. It costs $200 to $500.

It finishes last because height does not add capacity: the same 550 lb figure now spreads across 30 units, so a full rack must be built of light gear. A tall, narrow rack on casters also needs care, since it can wobble if it is overloaded at the top. It suits large patch panel installations, where most devices weigh little.

Buy it for a big cabling room with many patch panels and switches. For anything heavy, the GlobalRack's 1200 lb rating is better.
cons: Capacity does not grow with height
products.idealFor: Large patch panel and switch installations with light gear.

methodology.title: Depth range
methodology.description: We compared usable and adjustable depth, since it decides whether a rack can hold deep servers or only shallow network gear.

methodology.title: Load rating
methodology.description: We separated ratings for feet, casters and wall mounting, and treated the lowest applicable figure as the real limit.

methodology.title: Frame construction
methodology.description: We looked at steel gauge, riveted versus bolted joints and hole style, which affect rigidity and compatibility.

methodology.title: Mobility and mounting
methodology.description: We considered casters, wall mount options and weight, since racks often have to move for cabling.

methodology.title: Included hardware and value
methodology.description: We weighed shelves, grounding wires, cable rings and hardware kits against each price bracket.

whatMatters.detail: Depth is the space between the front and rear mounting rails, and equipment must fit inside it. Switches are shallow, but rack servers often need 24 to 30 inches or more. Check the deepest device you own, add room for cables behind it, and choose a rack with adjustable depth if unsure.

One rack unit (1U) is 1.75 inches of vertical space, so a 12U rack has 21 inches of mounting height. Plan for the devices you have plus about 30 percent spare. Remember that a UPS, shelves and cable management also take units.

The load rating is the weight the rack can safely carry. It changes with how the rack sits: feet carry more than casters, and a wall mount carries the least. Use the lowest applicable figure and keep heavy items near the bottom.

Square holes take cage nuts, and threaded or round holes take screws directly. Cage nuts make mounting and removing equipment easier. Check which pattern the rack uses and whether the right screws, such as M6, are included.

Locking casters let you roll the rack out for cabling and then fix it in place. Tall racks on casters can tip if overloaded, and the rolling rating is lower than the static one. Look for locking wheels and a stated rolling capacity.

howToChoose.intro: Measure the deepest piece of gear you own, then add a few inches for cables and airflow.

cards.label: Fixed depth
cards.text: Simple, usually sturdier for the money, and fine for switches and patch panels. You cannot adapt later. Picks: AxcessAbles racks and Tecmojo.

cards.label: Adjustable depth
cards.text: Slides the rear rails to match deep servers or shallow switches. A little more setup and a larger footprint. Picks: VEVOR 12U and 20U, GlobalRack, RIVECO.

howToChoose.note: Choose adjustable depth if there is any chance you will add a server.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Adjustable depth, casters, a grounding wire and square holes. Keep heavy gear at the bottom and leave room for airflow.

cards.label: In this ranking
cards.text: The VEVOR 12U suits a first lab, and the GlobalRack 27U gives you room when the lab grows.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You carry heavy servers or want a permanent, rigid frame. The RIVECO 25U or GlobalRack 27U earns it.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You have only network gear. The VEVOR 12U or Tecmojo covers it for $50 to $100.

faq.q: Will a server fit in an 18 inch deep rack?
faq.a: Almost never. Rack servers are typically 24 to 30 inches deep or more, so an 18 inch rack is for switches and patch panels. Check the server's depth in its specifications before you buy a rack.

faq.q: What is the most common mistake with budget racks?
faq.a: Looking only at the headline capacity. Ratings differ for feet, casters and wall mounts, and some titles advertise a higher figure than the spec. Use the lowest applicable rating.

faq.q: Is an open frame worth it over an enclosed cabinet?
faq.a: It is if you want airflow, easy access and a low price. An enclosed cabinet is quieter and keeps dust out, but costs more and needs ventilation. Many home labs use an open frame in a closet.

faq.q: How do I set up the rack safely?
faq.a: Assemble it on a flat floor, level the feet, and lock the casters. Mount the heaviest gear at the bottom. Connect the grounding wire if one is included.

faq.q: Can I mount a rack on a wall?
faq.a: Some models, like the Tecmojo and VEVOR, list a wall capacity, and it is lower than the floor rating. You need studs or proper masonry anchors. Keep the load well under the stated figure.
Leave gaps between hot devices, keep the rear clear and avoid sealing the rack in a closet. Vented panels help. A small fan can improve airflow for hot equipment.

finalTake: The VEVOR 12U Open Frame Server Rack is the best budget server rack for most people, because it fits both shallow and deep gear and includes casters and a ground wire. The GlobalRack 27U is the one to buy for a larger lab, and the RIVECO 25U suits permanent, heavy installs. The AxcessAbles racks work well for network gear only.
